oneLineAnswer: Brentuximab vedotin is a prescription cancer drug given into a vein, not a supplement.
whatItIs: Brentuximab vedotin is a prescription cancer medicine sold under the brand name Adcetris. It belongs to a group called antibody-drug conjugates. In this design, a lab-made antibody carries a cell-killing chemical to cancer cells. The antibody part is built to stick to CD30, a protein found on the surface of certain lymphoma cells. The chemical part, MMAE, is a microtubule inhibitor. Microtubules are rope-like structures that cells need in order to divide. A linker joins the two parts and releases the chemical once the drug is inside a cell. The product is a powder that is mixed into a liquid and given into a vein. It was first approved in the United States in 2011.
whatItDoes: The antibody part binds CD30, the cell pulls the pair inside, and the linker releases MMAE.
MMAE attaches to tubulin and breaks up the microtubule network, which stops cells dividing and kills them.
CD30 is common on Hodgkin lymphoma cells and on many anaplastic large cell lymphoma cells.
Approved uses include Hodgkin lymphoma, several T-cell lymphomas, mycosis fungoides and some large B-cell lymphomas.
In one trial in relapsed large B-cell lymphoma, adding it to two other drugs was linked to longer survival than those drugs alone.
howPeopleUseIt: The label describes it as a 30-minute infusion into a vein, given in a clinic or hospital.
Schedules in the label repeat the infusion every three weeks for a planned number of cycles.
It is often combined with chemotherapy drugs, and some approved uses are as a single drug.
Trials have tested it alone and alongside other cancer treatments, such as lenalidomide and rituximab.
People receiving it may also be given G-CSF, a medicine that supports white blood cell counts.

commonSideEffects: Nerve damage, called peripheral neuropathy, is the most common problem; it usually shows as numbness or tingling in the hands or feet.
Fatigue, nausea, diarrhoea, constipation, vomiting, fever, muscle or joint pain, mouth sores, abdominal pain and rash each occurred in at least one in five people.
Upper respiratory infections and cough were also common.
Blood tests often showed low neutrophils, low haemoglobin, low lymphocytes, raised glucose, raised creatinine and raised liver enzymes.
In the large B-cell lymphoma trial, pneumonia and COVID-19 infection were among the common side effects.
seriousSigns: The label carries a boxed warning for PML, a rare brain infection caused by the JC virus that has been fatal.
PML can show up as mood or behaviour changes, confusion, memory loss, or changes in vision, speech or walking.
Infusion reactions, including a severe allergic reaction called anaphylaxis, can happen during or shortly after an infusion.
The label tells people to report fever, chills, rash or breathing problems within 24 hours of an infusion.
Serious infections such as pneumonia, bloodstream infection and sepsis, including fatal cases, have been reported.
Tumour lysis syndrome can occur in people whose tumours are fast-growing or bulky.
Liver injury, lung inflammation, severe skin reactions, pancreatitis and high blood sugar were also reported.
whoShouldAvoid: It must not be given with bleomycin, because that combination can damage the lungs.
The label says to avoid it in people with severe kidney impairment.
It is also avoided in moderate or severe liver impairment, with a lower dose if liver impairment is mild.
It can harm a fetus, so it is not used during pregnancy.
Breastfeeding is not recommended while it is being given.
In children, its use is established only for those aged 2 and older with a certain high-risk Hodgkin lymphoma.

interactions: CYP3A4 is a liver enzyme that breaks down many medicines, including the MMAE part of this drug.
Ketoconazole, a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor, raised exposure to MMAE when the two were given together.
The label says to watch closely for side effects when a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor is used at the same time.
Strong CYP3A4 inducers may also change MMAE levels, though the label gives no separate instructions for them.
It should not be mixed with, or infused at the same time as, other medicines.
Bleomycin is the one medicine the label rules out completely.
pregnancyAndChildren: In pregnant rats, brentuximab vedotin caused harm to the developing fetus, including malformations, at exposures similar to the human dose. The label says the human pregnancy data come only from case reports and are not enough to judge risk, so it advises a pregnant woman of a possible risk to the fetus. Women who could become pregnant are asked to use effective contraception during treatment and for two months after the last dose. Men with female partners who could become pregnant are asked to use contraception during treatment and for four months after, because the drug may damage sperm and testicular tissue. There is no information on whether it passes into human milk, and breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment. In children, safety and effectiveness are established only for those aged 2 and older with previously untreated high-risk Hodgkin lymphoma, given with chemotherapy. It is not established for younger children or for other uses.
whatWeDoNotKnow: There are no human data on whether brentuximab vedotin passes into breast milk.
Pregnancy information rests on case reports, which the label calls insufficient to judge risk.
Carcinogenicity studies have not been done for the drug or for the MMAE chemical.
No fertility studies exist for the drug or for MMAE, so human effects on fertility are unknown.
Effects in children younger than 2 have not been established, and no results are cited for that age group.
PubChem holds substance entries for brentuximab vedotin but no single compound record, because it is a conjugate rather than one small molecule.
The label's interaction section covers only CYP3A4 inhibitors and the bleomycin contraindication, so other drug combinations are not described.
No dose amounts appear in this record by design; it reports only what the label states about how the medicine is given.
Only one effectiveness trial is summarised here, from the FDA notice for relapsed large B-cell lymphoma; other clinical study sections were not reviewed in full.
